#3882. Amid soaring PC hardware prices, gaming monitors are getting cheaper and cheaper. Here's why, and what to buy

Hello, good local-time-zone-adjusted afternoon, and let's just say it's been a while. But I come back to you now at the turn of the technological tide. Well, sort of. Sadly I'm not here to predict an end to the ridiculous AI-fuelled chip crisis. That whole mess has a couple of years to run, surely.

Instead I speak of screens, where there is actually some very good news. In short, have you seen how cheap PC gaming monitors are? I mean remarkably, almost stupendously, cheap. I'm talking £60 / $60 for an entry-level 1080p panel with triple-digit refresh rate, sub-£200 / $250 for high-refresh 4K gaming. Heck, even OLED monitors now start with a "2" in both currencies.

Also bear in mind we've had a fair old bit of inflation in recent years. A 4K panel bought today for £200 is equivalent to paying roughly £150 back in 2020. All the while, that same £200 / $200 right now won't buy you a current-model gaming graphics card at all, even the most feeble example, and will barely secure a basic dual-channel 16GB DDR5 memory kit. Youch.

So, I think we can all agree monitors are cheap in the current chip-catastrophe context. The immediate question is why? The answer isn't all that complicated, actually. Most obviously, the display market isn't being devoured by the AI craze. All those data centres are stuffed with GPUs, memory chips and NAND flash, not monitors.

By way of example, one of the largest new AI data centres on Earth is Microsoft's new Fairwater site in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin. It's thought to pack hundreds of thousands of Nvidia Blackwell GPUs. The cost doesn't bear thinking about, but those GPUs are built into what's known as "headless" server racks. In other words, they have no screens at all. Ultimately, the key compute hardware is all managed remotely, in which capacity the Fairwater facility is reported to currently have around 375 employees. If we generously assume each has two PC monitors, that's only 750 for the entire site.

AI isn't really driving demand on the end-user side of the equation, either. Put it this way: you don't need to buy a new phone, laptop or PC to access the latest models. At the same time, the display market is suffering from something of a glut of overcapacity. Chinese companies built out huge capacity in LCD panel manufacturing over the past decade, to the extent factories are now running underutilised. Meanwhile, even the OLED market is arguably oversupplied.

In fact, Samsung and LG, the two big noises in large OLED panel manufacturing (as opposed to OLED displays for tablets and phones), have been shifting emphasis away from TV panels to PC monitors because the latter offer better margins. Meanwhile, the AI boom has almost definitely meant lower demand for new PCs. Certainly, the big research houses point to cratering PC sales thanks to higher component costs. Long story short, that's oodles of capacity combined with weakening demand. Like I said, the explanation for cheap monitors isn't exactly rocket surgery, if you know what I mean.

What is a bit more complicated is making sense of what's available today in the gaming monitor market. With so much choice, where exactly is the very best value to be found? And are there any remaining pain points?

Monitor specifications, to be sure, can be tricksy at the best of times. But if you're looking for some blanket rules to fling casually over the whole LCD monitor market - I'll be digging deeper into OLED tech another day - try these for size. Look for, at minimum, 300 nits brightness and 1ms response times. Refresh rates are a slightly more complicated call, but for the vast majority of games, 144Hz is plenty. For "esports-grade multiplayer fare like Counter-Strike or Dota 2, or I think a refresh in the high 200s will get the job done for most. If you'll benefit from more than that, you almost certainly know who you are already.

Oh, and heavily favour IPS over VA panels. Exceptions exist: there are some decent "Rapid VA" panels these days and Samsung, in particular, does some nippy VA models. But a lot of the cheaper stuff is pretty slow and smeary, making VA a risky buy. Finally, don't worry too much about claimed HDR capability, save for the fact that HDR 400 certification at least means the monitor can do 400 nits. Unless a monitor has local dimming, it won't be truly HDR capable.

Anywho, one immediate and rather ironic issue is the growing mismatch between monitors and GPUs. For sure, it's great you can grab a high-refresh 4K monitor for such little money. It's almost hard to believe that you can have this 27-inch IPS MSI for sub-£200 (you're looking at $250 for the same model in the US), and it even has a 288Hz 1080p dual mode.

I actually favour 32 inches with my 4K gaming, and that's naturally a little pricier, especially if you insist on an IPS - which again, you probably should. But even $350 for that kind of panel (here's a comparable model for £340 in the UK) is a fraction of what you'd have paid for a similarly specced model a few years ago. And it probably wouldn't have included dual-mode functionality.

Here's the problem, though. How are you going to drive the thing, what with its eight million-plus pixels? After all, the cheapest RTX 5090 on Newegg right now is over $6,500. So high-end Nvidia GPUs now cost about as much as a decent used car.

Of course, you might be surprised just how effective the likes of an AMD RX 9070 XT or Nvidia RTX 5070-class GPU is at 4K thanks to upscaling technologies including DLSS and FSR. The latest transformer model upscalers really do knock out pretty stellar image quality. Add in a bit of frame gen and you have a compelling combination of visual sharpness, reasonably low latency and nice smoothframe rates, even in the most demanding of games. Perhaps the one thing you can't do is enable full path tracing in a game like Cyberpunk 2077 and still expect a slick experience, but standard ray tracing remains an option.

The bigger snag, unsurprisingly, is that you can no longer bag a 5070 at (let alone below) its original £539 / $549 MSRP. Instead, you're looking at the thick end of £800 / $900. That's a bit of an ask for pairing with a £200 monitor, isn't it?

I'd therefore argue that, for pure gaming purposes, the bang-for-buck sweet spot remains just where it's been sat twiddling its thumbs for the better part of a decade, namely 1440p. That applies to both its vanilla 16:9 aspect variety and my personally preferred ultrawide format, the latter being so very immersive and also pretty nifty for daily multi-tasking. Indeed, the 27-inch 1440p segment even brings the vibrant colours and infinite contrast of OLED panels into a reasonably affordable window.

By way of example, £179 (or $150) is enough for a circa 200Hz, IPS 1440p panel with super low (by IPS standards) pixel response, even if the 250-nit brightness is lower than I'd like. Meanwhile, as I write these words, pricing for big-brand 27-inch 1440p gaming OLEDs kicks off at about £290 in the UK and roughly $270 in the US. Admittedly, those entry-level OLEDs come with some compromises, which I'll cover in a forthcoming post. But what you might call 'proper' OLED panels can be had around the low £300 / $300 mark - not throw-away money, for sure, but relatively accessible.

The 34-inch 1440p ultrawide segment is a bit trickier, however. The good news is that conventional LCD models can be had for relative peanuts, with prices starting at about £220 or $249 for game-focused, high-refresh models. But those two example both use a VA panel, which usually means inferior pixel response.

IPS models are a little thin on the ground when it comes to 34-inch ultrawide, but sneaking in below £300 / $300 is generally possible. The real bummer is OLED, where going ultrawide invokes a massive premium. The best price I can find on a big-brand 34-inch ultrawide today is $629 for this Asus model in the US and £648 for this MSI option in the UK.

That's awfully toppy, especially when you consider that you can grab a 49-inch, 5,120x1,440 ultrawide OLED for barely any more money. I do actually quite like those 49-inch ultrawides, but I have to concede the ergonomics are challenging. However, 4K OLEDs in 27-inch and 32-inch formats can also be had for as much as £100 / $100 less than the current cheapest 34-inch 1440p ultrawides, which doesn't make much sense to me.

Again, with 4K, there's the challenge of keeping all those pixels updated. If you already have a sufficiently mighty graphics card, though, I a 32-inch 4K OLED can make a fantastic all-round option, and something like this MSI model for £549 would be absolutely lovely. You get good pixel density and lots of space for daily desktopping, plus OLED visuals and a large enough panel to be really get you into your games.

It's just a pity that 34-inch OLED ultrawides remain so weirdly expensive, it being a format that ticks so many different boxes. As for my own personal money-no-object pick, well, I'm typing these words on the new Alienware AW3926QW, the 39-inch 5K2K beast with a Tandem WOLED panel and RGB subpixels.

One could argue it's a relative steal at £1,079 or $1,100. I mean, it's pretty much peak current PC gaming display technology, and it's about half the price of what Nvidia's second-tier RTX 5080 graphics card is going for lately. Assuming you can even find one in stock.

At this point, the one major category I haven't covered is LCD monitors with mini-LED full-array local dimming. Cards on the table, I'm not a huge fan of mini-LED monitors. The detailed reasons for that are, perhaps, the subject for another day. But I've reviewed countless models and have yet to see one that didn't come with pretty serious compromises.

That said, the technology has gotten a lot more accessible in the last 12 to 18 months, to the extent that 27-inch 1440p models start at just over $250. I've had that specific model in and came away pretty impressed. It's very, very punchy, and even factoring in the limitations of mini-LED versus OLED when it comes to lighting control and speed, I cannot deny the temptation.

Just for completeness, one further exception to the general rule of cheap gaming monitors involves ultra-high refresh monitors aimed at serious esports aficionados. I'm talking about panels like this 1,000Hz LG I sampled elsewhere. At £800 / $1,000 for a 25-inch 1080p IPS panel it's inevitably a niche proposition, and poor value by normal standards.

I think a much better compromise for just about everyone, short of an actual esports pro, is to grab a larger, higher resolution monitor that offers one of those windowed 1080p modes running at about 500Hz or thereabouts. That way you've got a nice high-res panel for both work and play, as well as that ultra-low latency mode for when you want to dance around Dust 2 doling out the headshots or whatever.

Incidentally, I realise I've gone in a bit hot and heavy with the OLED content here, the implicit assumption being OLED is all that, and notably without addressing the obvious objections like the risk of burn-in. But all that, I hope you'll be pleased to hear, is very much the subject for my next RPS post on all things OLED.

Until then, all I can say is thank goodness PC monitors provide relative respite from the parlous state of much of the rest of the PC component market. It's absolutely brutal out there if you're building a gaming PC, but at least you'll get a lot of screen for your money.

Just to round things out, if anyone has any specific queries at any given price point, form factor or panel type, shout out below and I'll try to steer you in the direction of a decent model.

#3881. Fantasy RPG 'Sovereign Tower' Brings Some Round Table Management To Switch Next Year

Sovereign Tower launched on Steam earlier this year and quickly picked up its fair share of fans for its wacky round table management. Today, developer Wild Wits and publisher Curve Games have announced that we Switch fans will be able to get in on the fun in the new year.

That's right, this one is coming to Switch on 14th January 2027. In it, you play as the sovereign of the titular tower, thrust into power after the untimely demise of your predecessor and tasked with keeping the kingdom up and running. To do so, you'll have to recruit knights and match their unique skills to tasks across the land — nabbing stolen manuscripts, taking down evil beings, negotiating with vampires, you know the drill.

There's a rewind function for when things go south, and you can even romance some of those handsome knights you'll meet along the way.

Here's a brief rundown of its key features and a handful of screens so you can soak in the cool visuals:

Your Reign, Your Rules - Every choice you make defines your legacy and the fate of your kingdom. Recruit eccentric Knights - Manage a court of unpredictable heroes with big egos and even bigger problems. Manage Your Round Table - Send knights on epic quests where success or disaster hinges on your judgment. Bend Time and Tempt Fate - Uncover secrets, pursue forbidden romances, and when it all goes wrong, rewind time like they never happened in the first place. Expand Your Tower - Build new annexes, acquire upgrades, and outwit rival rulers in increasingly impressive displays of sovereignty.

January is already filling up with Switch releases, but this could just end up being one to look out for.

Will you be checking out Sovereign Tower on Switch next year? Let us know in the comments.

#3880. The next Xbox, Project Helix, is a console and "not a PC" says Microsoft, as it clarifies that computational power isn't sole focus this time

"It is about leveraging new technical advancements such as neural rendering."

Microsoft has stressed that its next-generation Xbox console, Project Helix, "is not a PC that can also play console games", but rather "a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC". The company has also underlined the importance of using gen-AI-adjacent "neural rendering" technology going forwards, and a desire to remove "all the barriers of play that have historically existed" - notably in making the past generations of games playable.

The details come from a Microsoft-produced Xbox magazine made available digitally yesterday, and a Helix-related feature speaking to Xbox vice president of next generation, Jason Ronald. "When we think about Project Helix, it's really designed to be the ultimate gaming machine," Ronald said, "one that removes all the barriers of play that have historically existed. My entire library is accessible to me. I'm able to bring four generations of my Xbox library and progression with me and have it available instantly. And we remove the arbitrary constraints between console and PC games.

"We're very clear on the design goal," Ronald later added. "Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games. The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access my games. But if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customisability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it."

Notably, Ronald seemed to suggest that Helix - the console, not the handheld; "Helix" refers to a couple of machines - isn't solely focused on computational grunt. Indeed, he said the next generation wasn't about hitting 8K resolutions and 240 hertz frame-rates, but instead leaning on technologies like "neural rendering" - i.e. generative-AI - and encouraging innovation.

"It's about deeper immersion," Ronald said. "It is about leveraging new technical advancements such as neural rendering to deliver a new level of visual fidelity in more efficient and innovative ways. It's about new kinds of games and new game experiences that we haven't been able to do before. What excites me about the future is the idea of entirely new types of games that have never been possible before, delivered through all the innovation in the silicon and the hardware and the platform that we're delivering."

While referencing the global component shortage and exorbitant prices of computer hardware, he added: "This is a big reason why we're really focused on advancements like neural rendering because it's an entirely new way to generate a frame without requiring more computational horsepower, additional memory, and things like that. I think you're going to see more innovation over the next three to five years than you've seen in the last 10 years."

Xbox boss Asha Sharma also recently talked up the importance of generative-AI-sounding technology in Xbox's future, saying "too many ideas never become games", and that "a single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations".

Another key part of Xbox's Helix vision is compatibility and game preservation. "Game preservation is core to Xbox," Ronald went as far as to say. "Not only do we feel like it's the right thing for the industry, we feel a deep responsibility as one of its biggest platforms and publishers. For the first 30 years of game development, nobody really thought about game preservation when they were designing their hardware, when they were building their games." Xbox is apparently working with game-makers to ensure games can not only be played now but also 20 to 30 years into the future.

The other key facet of Microsoft's push the familiar Play Anywhere mantra, whereby one game can be played across multiple devices, maintaining your game-progress as you go. This is fundamental to Microsoft's handheld-and-console Helix plan, and something we've seen the company dry-run with the Xbox ROG Ally X handheld. "It's this notion that not only does my library move with me, but my progress moves with me as well," Ronald said. "Because I fully expect that when I'm in the middle of an 80-hour RPG, if I'm 25 hours into that and I want to play it on another device, I should be able to instantly resume from where I was. Those are things that today are becoming more common, but I think in the future it's going to be a baseline expectation of all players."

Ronald wouldn't be drawn on the issue of price regarding Project Helix - a recent report suggested Helix could be priced up to $1800 - referring to it only as both "a challenging time" but an "exciting one", because "we have to invent entirely new technology to continue to advance the state-of-the-art while also continuing to make things accessible and affordable". Ronald also wouldn't reference a release date, though the report referenced above suggested the handheld Helix machine will release next holiday, 2027, and the console Helix machine the year after. The next generation, then, seems to be around the corner.

#3879. Nvidia board reportedly prepare to give CEO Jensen Huang the boot, as second alleged affair thrusts him closer to seriously lusty Crusader Kings playthrough territory

The next step's usually a desperately initiated sway scheme

The situation at the highest levels of AI and also some graphics cards if you insist company Nvidia continues to look, well, less than ideal. CEO Jensen Huang, he of the reported extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, now appears to potentially be on the verge of being chucked out of the window of a black and green corporate tower, following a report claiming that he had a second alleged affair with an executive who reports to him.

The New York Times report that Huang's second alleged extramarital affair was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, responsible for the company's tech being adopted in the medical field for the likes of imaging and aiding in drug discovery. If that's the case, at least this time there won't be any strongly-worded denials of espionage from the Chinese government, though it would still very much be an internal nightmare for Nvidia.

So, Huang has so far not caused more than one international incident with his alleged infidelity. Still, Nvidia's board are reportedly preparing to oust the CEO from his post. That's according to the Wall Street Journal, with other publications currently only going as far as reporting that the board are weighing up whether to give Huang the boot.

Earlier this week, Nvidia shareholders filed a lawsuit in California against the company over claims that they were misled regarding Huang's alleged affair with the suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia's shares have dipped following the reports of the alleged affairs.

With Huang potentially poised to go, chatter about possible successors has already kicked off. Elon Musk, meanwhile, has taken to the social media hellscape he owns to suggest he'd be up for hiring Huang if the exec is ousted from Nvidia. Epic Games boss Tim Sweeney is also on there calling for Huang's job to be saved, because of course he is.

The question all of this has left me with, aside from wondering why people in real world power insist on behaving like they've gotten a bit bored in the middle of a Crusader Kings 3 session, is this: is there someone on hand who can try to describe 63-year-old nerdy businessman Jensen Huang like he's some sort of irresistibly sexy heartthrob? "Huang isn't the usual CEO. He is a charismatic, leather-jacket-wearing apostle of Nvidia chips who built the company on processors for video games, transformed it into an artificial intelligence machine, and, in turn, created the most valuable company in the world."

#3877. Can GTA 6 make $2 billion in its opening weekend? One industry analyst has run the numbers, and seems to think so

We all know the story of GTA 5 making more than $1 billion in the first three days it was on sale, right? At the time, Take-Two believed this to be the fastest any entertainment property had achieved the impressive milestone - music and films included. It made history, and with ease. And it looks like GTA 6 is going to do even better.

At least, that's according to one analyst, Joost van Dreunen, a senior data analyst and great writer/numbers diviner who wrote some predictions in his respected SuperJoost PlayList newsletter. "My prediction: Take-Two announces opening-weekend sales above $2 billion by Monday, 23rd November," he wrote. And you know what? I reckon he's onto something.

Let's review what we already know: there is a conservative estimate of 10 million pre-orders for Rockstar's latest game floating around - something buoyed by comments from Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick - and, even by the company's lofty expectations, we know the game is tracking "well above expectations" when it comes to pre-orders.

We also know a lot of people are shelling out for the slightly more pricey Ultimate Edition (£90). So many people are opting for the more expensive version, in fact, that Take-Two revised its financial forecast up to $3.5bn for the next financial quarter, thanks to "recurrent consumer spending" (something Zelnick clarified in an investor's call is explicitly linked to the Ultimate Edition). 10 million pre-orders, at roughly $100 per copy - that's $1 billion right off the bat.

"That’s two days faster than its predecessor," van Dreunen said, "and largely before anyone has even played the game." That other $1bn will come over the weekend. And then, per the analyst, the game will sell roughly another 28 million copies over the course of the first year it's on sale. "My forecast puts first-year sales at 38 million copies, only modestly ahead of GTA 5’s 35 million. The real difference may be how much revenue each player generates over the years that follow."

But it's what follows in the newsletter that intrigues me most. "At the high end, [GTA 6] may just lift the entire industry with it," wrote van Dreunen. "In the face of AI slop and shitty mobile games that exist only to extract revenue, it will offer a reprieve. At a time when the industry is increasingly focused on making games cheaper and monetising players more aggressively, Rockstar is about to demonstrate the enduring appeal of spending a fortune to make something people actually want to play."

So, even if you're dubious about the game and Rockstar's motivations for selling as many copies as possible, the launch of GTA 6 could be something that gives the industry a much-needed jolt of life, in the face of rampant layoffs and shrinking talent pools.

It's not all sunshine and rainbows ahead for Rockstar, though: amongst the frenzy of launch activity, Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week, as the game goes on sale.

#3876. Nvidia boss Jensen Huang resigns amid scandal surrounding two alleged affairs, interim CEO appointed as search for sexy leather jacket man's successor begins

Guess his desperately initiated sway scheme failed, then.

Nvidia have ripped off the wax strip and are looking for a new CEO. Jensen Huang, he of the reported extramarital affairs with both a suspected Chinese spy and one of his executive underlings at Nvidia has removed his bottom from the great throne of black and green graphics cards.

"Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately," Nvidia declared in a press release announcing the "CEO transition" they're embarking on. Stepping up to replace Huang for the immediate future is current Nvidia executive vice president and chief financial officer Colette Kress, who is becoming interim CEO on top of her established number-crunching duties.

One would assume she's quickly calculated just how much extra work Jensen's alleged inability to not get amorous with women who aren't his wife will add to her plate until a permanent successor is found. Speaking of that, Nvidia wrote that they "will consider internal and external candidates" in their scanning for someone to step into Huang's leather jacket. Actually, Nvidia folks, maybe don't let the new person wear the leather jacket, lest people potentially find them dangerously attractive. Failing that, maybe a pair of padlocked underpants are in order, adorned with flashing green lights to ensure brand recognition in trouserless scenarios.

The company's board of directors have gone ahead and appointed Harvey Jones as their first ever chairperson, one would assume to help convince money people that they've got strong enough leadership in place until their new permanent boss is found.

"Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," interim CEO Kress said "We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders." Oh, come on, think how many people would cheer if you said you fancied pivoting even a tiny bit of attention away from AI and back to consumer GPUs.

"Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound," the company's release concluded. "Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

Goodbye, leather jacket man who was allegedly too sexy for his own good, despite being a nerd who stands on stages waving hardware about. Odds are we'll see you again, possibly in the company of Elon Musk, because execs can never be allowed to be out of lucrative work for more than five minutes.

As GTA 6 players progress through the plot and explore beyond the sunny shores of Key Lento, bunny boiler Mandy has been left behind.

It’s all about Delights’ resident goth girl Vicki now!

The character plays a bit-part during Chapter 2, and she’s quickly become a fave among PS5 players for her husky voice and no-nonsense attitude.

Writing on X, one fan put it simply: “Oh yeah we on Vicki now, I don’t even know who Mandy is!”

Some have even taken to social media stalking the dancer on Snapmatic:

Simping aside, Vicki may actually sound familiar because her voice actor is Taryn Manning, who had a pretty major role as Tiffany ‘Pennsatucky’ Doggett in Orange Is the New Black.

The 48-year-old actress has also starred in a variety of other shows like Sons of Anarchy, and has even had parts in movies like Hustle & Flow and the 8-Mile.

There are a lot of characters to keep track of in GTA 6, but Vicki is definitely one that stuck with me, largely because she’s pivotal to one of my favourite missions in the game.

(I won’t spoil that here, but if you’re grinning you’ll probably know which one I’m referring to.)

I’m not going to get into the Vicki vs Mandy debate, but I’m sure social media will have its final say eventually.

#3873. Ever wanted to play a multiplayer version of Cyberpunk 2077 with your friends? Well, thanks to a mod now in beta, you can

You may have recently read that CD Projekt Red's in-development Cyberpunk 2 may be trying to revive the original game's online ambitions. But, if you don't want to wait the many years it'll likely be before the Cyberpunk 2077 sequel arrives, then I've got good news for you: Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer mod CyberMP is now out in open beta.

"After almost six years of development, countless reworks, and code rewrites, we're finally launching the public beta," the modders on the CyberMP Discord channel wrote (thanks RPS). "Anyone can jump in and play now - no invites or applications needed." The team notes, however, that this is "true beta", meaning "Crashes, desyncs, and server drops under heavy load are completely normal for now. That's exactly why we need testers."

Alongside the potential shakiness, the devs say it's also possible the mod could ping your anti-virus software, since it "doesn't have a digital signature yet". Whilst the priorities for the team lie in "polishing the foundations" and "fixing crashes and stability", more features are eventually planned. But for now, they stress, "let's see how the project handles real player traffic!"

So, what exactly is it? CyberMP is a dedicated multiplayer modification for Cyberpunk 2077 that allows you and your friends to explore Night City together: drive vehicles, engage in combat, and play custom community-created game modes on high-tick dedicated servers. You need an official copy of the game to play it (obviously), and the mod is completely free to download. You can download the mod, and read a fair amount of how to get it working, what to expect from it, and how to troubleshoot any issues, over at its dedicated website.

If you're thinking 'Hang on, why does Cyberpunk 2077 multiplayer sound so familiar?', it's because the game was supposed to receive an official multiplayer mode after its original release. Thanks to its shaky launch, however, plans changed, and CD Projekt Red later announced that multiplayer would be a separate "triple-A release", but, eventually, that too was cancelled. The studio is still keen to honour the idea, though, and recently stated it's "focusing on bringing online into all of our franchises one day".

This isn't the first big bit of news we've had about Cyberpunk 2077 mods this week. Just yesterday, a new mod called 'Torrent' added 3D rain, lightning storms, and tyre spray to Night City - all rendered and made lovely with a new lighting system that seems to play nicely with other weather mods that have been created for the game.

#3872. Jensen Huang Has Been Reinstated As Nvidia's President And CEO

Company produces custom processor for Switch 2

Update [Mon 23rd Nov 2026, 2:20pm]: Nvidia has posted an update confirming that Jensen Huang has now been reinstated as president, CEO, and board member following his earlier resignation.

The post confirms that Nvidia's board "received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk".

Huang resigned following multiple instances of alleged infidelity, most notably with an alleged Chinese spy, leading to concerns over national security as the US and China butt heads in the race to become the dominant force in the world of AI.

Huang also contributed the following message

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution. I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period.

"I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”

We can only assume that the investigation into Huang's relationships turned up nothing unusual – surely they wouldn't just sweep it under the rug, right?

Meanwhile, US president Donald Trump celebrated Huang's reinstatement, calling him a "Great Patriot and National Treasure" while stating that the decision is vital to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy".

Original Story: Nvidia, one of the largest tech firms in the world and the company responsible for the Switch 2's custom processor, has found itself embroiled in scandal over recent days.

As reported by The Guardian, Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, who you might recognise from the 'Creator's Voice Special Edition' video for Switch 2, has now resigned after reported affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee.

He will be replaced on an interim basis by Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, until a full-time successor is named. Nvidia's share price began to sharply decline following reports of the scandal, to the point where it is now no longer the most valuable company in the world.

The BBC speculates that Huang's departure could set him up to be a "formidable opponent" to the very company he co-founded, with Elon Musk stating that it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX.

With regards to Nintendo, it's likely that none of this will have any immediate impact on Nvidia's relationship with the Japanese company. Nvidia will no doubt be under contract to supply custom chips for the Switch 2, but what happens with the inevitable Switch 2 successor is under question.

Hopefully everything will go smoothly for Nintendo, but if it wants to utilise Nvidia's architecture for its next console – particularly for backwards compatibility – then its efforts may be impacted by Huang's departure along with Nvidia's sharp pivot towards AI.

Of course, it's really early to be speculating about the 'Switch 3', but you can bet that Nintendo's R&D department will be looking at all of this very closely and considering its potential impact.

#3871. The hills are alive with The Sound of Fury, a fantasy musical hack 'n' slash about weaponising pianos to fight the Devil

My firstest-ever Golden Joystick Awards, which took place last night in London, was marred somewhat by 1) a gin & tonic costing eleven quid and 2) my view of the stage being directly obscured by its own rigging. Nonetheless, I did crane enough to get a good view at the reveal of The Sound of Fury, a musically-minded hack 'n' slash in which a troubled classical musician descends into Hell to save a friend from the Devil.

It's not out until late 2027, and the strength of its monster-battering will of course lay in how it feels in the hand. I like the look of this one, though. While it doesn't appear to be a full-on rhythm action game in the Hi-Fi Rush or Dead as Disco vein, it's clearly trying incorporate our glum hero's virtuosity with both visual and thematic flair: spinning attacks are accentuated by trails of sheet music staves, and at least one move inflicts enemies with uncontrollable bouts of dancing. Weapons also take the form of instruments, the trailer being particularly keen to show grand pianos being powerbombed into demon heads. "You dropped your... keys," I will say, to the demons. Heh heh heh.

Also of note is The Sound of Fury's unusual interpretation of Hell, which rather than the usual Biblical/Nordic/Ancient Greek depictions we get in games, is a washed-out mashup of what the Steam page calls "humanity's darkest chapters." Thus, you fight not red-skinned horned imps but gasmasked soldiers and Klu Klux Klansmen, with history-spanning anomalies distorting an otherwise 19th century-flavoured fantasyscape. The laws of time evidently aren't followed here, not least when the protag whips out a Flying V guitar to give the Grim Reaper a different kind of axe wound.

I can't find much else out about developers and self-publishers Games By Wojtek, with that pluralisation assuming 'they' aren't just one person named Wojtek, but The Sound of Fury looks to be his/their debut game. Hopefully it gets a demo, in due course, so we can try tickling its ivories ourselves.

#3870. World of Warcraft: Forever completionists push back as Blizzard gives them a powerful toy and then prepares to take it away

"Exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors."

With the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever there's a whole new world filled with niche gear and strange baubles to collect. But one item in particular has drawn the ire of the creators of a popular completionist add-on.

That add-on is All the Things, a must-install for collectors like me, as it acts as a database of all the gear, mounts, titles, crafting recipes, and super rare drops in the game. Once you collect something, it is hidden in the add-on, thus tracking your progress and making for a fantastic tool for picking the game apart.

On occasion, specific items have written notes attached by the All the Things development team, as is true of a special World of Warcraft: Forever toy, the Pouch of Violet Dust. This is a promotional item that was obtainable by watching two hours of WoW Forever streams between the 4th and 12th November.

It's a powerful toy! When used on a campfire, it changes the fire's colour to purple and extends the buffs provided by it from the usual one hour to two hours. But the sticking point with the item isn't its existence, rather the fact that it's going to be removed in early December, not long from now.

This is what the creators of the All the Things add-on don't like. "A week-long, Twitch-only window for an item that gets taken away a month later is exactly the kind of FOMO that disheartens collectors," the creators said in a note attached to the item in the mod. "It can't be earned by playing the game at all. Even those who get it don't get to keep it."

They aren't alone in feeling this way. Comments below the item's listing on the Wowhead database are equally scorching. "I love FOMO in their explicitly non-fomo game," wrote user TheWhiteRose.

"Just... Why?" added user Darrenic427. "They could very easily just patch out the camp buff duration and keep the visual effect, but Blizzard just doesn't like pretty fire I guess. Figures that they finally give us access to purple fire but then take it away after a month."

The battle between collectors and time-limited FOMO items is one that has been waged for about as long as these sorts of items have been a part of games. Though for the pouch, it's an especially weird case: an item that's cool to have but so temporary in nature that it makes it both important to completionists and strangely pointless to care about. Whether it makes a return in a later update for World of Warcraft: Forever and doesn't require out-of-game actions to obtain, and doesn't disappear, we'll have to wait and see.

WoW Forever itself is proving popular among players - me included. It's added a staggering amount of new quests and many new features to the original version of World of Warcraft, which, in turn, has injected the game with an impressive amount of new items to collect. Completionists will likely be glued to the game for a long time.

#3869. Activision Dons Itself The Home Of Banjo-Kazooie In New Job Listing

"and now… Halo, Age of Empires, Sea of Thieves, and Banjo Kazooie"

Back in September, Xbox officially announced its reorganisation plans for legendary studio Rare, moving it under Activision alongside Halo, Age of Empires, Sea Of Thieves, and Banjo-Kazooie.

At the time, Rare was reportedly working on "other projects" beyond Sea of Thieves, but decisions about their future were now in Activision's hands. The two companies have collaborated pretty well in the past, considering how well Activision handled Crash Bandicoot and Spyro.

However, a new job posting on Activision's LinkedIn page suggests that another Rare IP, Banjo-Kazooie, has found a home amongst its new overseers. The job is for 'Product Manager, Emerging Franchises' with responsibilities to lead market planning, publishing strategies, drive business performance, and a whole bunch of other corporate fluff. What we found interesting is the accompanying mission statement.

Here's a look at the 'Your Mission' segment:

"Activision is home to iconic gaming franchises including Call of Duty®, Crash Bandicoot™, Spyro the Dragon™, and now… Halo®, Age of Empires®, Sea of Thieves™, and Banjo Kazooie®. Become part of the team working on building, growing, and shaping many of these franchises."

It's been a good 18 years since Banjo-Kazooie: Nuts & Bolts, already longer than GTA VI's 13-year wait, so you've gotta feel for Banjo fans. According to the job posting, both Sea of Thieves and Banjo-Kazooie now fall under Activision, with a team working on "building, growing, and shaping many of these franchises".

What happens next for Banjo-Kazooie has been a hot topic of conversation for donkeys now, and if this job listing is to be taken at face value, could we finally be looking at a new game in the near future? According to former Rare employee Grant Kirkhope, at least three studios have already pitched a new Banjo-Kazooie game to Microsoft. So, the interest is out there. Let's just wait and see what Activision does.

#3868. Cartoon-styled "lite-vania" Lola's Familiars: Prison of Argnoh will have you springing yourself, and your summoned pals, from magic jail

Andy Dufresne never thought to use witchcraft, did he

Since we're already sharing trailers from non-Geoff awards shows, here's another: a first in-motion look at Lola's Familiars: Prison of Argnoh, a 2D side-scroller and "lite-vania" that sees its shy witch-in-training making her first summonable friends. Then, borrowing their powers to bust out of a dark fantasy oubliette.

It looks like this'll be a mix of passively familiar-enhanced punching and more active, mayhaps traditionally Metroid-y power upgrades, Lola's ghastly pals looming over her tiny frame when called upon. It's all presented in a hand-drawn, lightly anime-ish style, complete with a story setup straight out of Saturday morning TV – Lola's only stuck in Skullcatraz because of a summoning-gone-wrong that occurred in pursuit of her school's unlikely Ofsted-compliant 'familiar contest'. I've attended school several times, and will attest that non-sporting contests, which students remain unaware of until seeing a poster for them, do not exist outside of childrens' television*.

This doesn't seem to be kid fodder, though. Lola's a bean but the familiars, and the prison's other denizens, are growling towers of jaws and decaying flesh. Developers Caracal Games are promising they'll star in a "heartfelt and emotionally resonant story about growth," to balance out the grimness, though I'm less clear on a following blurb point that declares it a "lite-vania," into which you'll "dive into exploration, trial-and-error and platforming, without feeling frustrated." While this might just be an attempt to assuage fears that this'll a Hollow Knight- or Nine Sols-style controller-thrower, I do wonder how one goes light on 'vania. Maybe some of the ability gates open if you just ask them nicely?

That aside, I'm already quite charmed by Lola's Familiars, especially the designs of its bag-eyed wallflower of a heroine and her contrastingly hench minions. Release date is TBC, but the Steam page is up.

*Granted, no TV example was ever as egregiously misleading as Jack Black vehicle School of Rock, which convinced me - then a barely-pubescent aspiring bassist - that winning a local Battle of the Bands would pay out thousands in cash, as opposed to the drinks rounds and packs of guitar strings I'd end up competing for a few years later.

#3867. GTA 6 Is Blowing Away Gaming's Greatest Devs, Including Naughty Dog

Industry professionals stunned by new sandbox

Naughty Dog’s Michael Barclay – whose credits include Uncharted: The Lost Legacy and The Last of Us 2 – says he’s “made video games for 19 years and GTA 6 appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child”.

Rockstar’s latest open world release is by far the best-looking game ever made, even if it is locked to 30fps on PS5 hardware.

And it’s being treated like witchcraft by devs, who naturally have a greater appreciation for the feats on display.

Barclay, who’s currently working on next year’s Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, continued:

“I'm always astonished that [Rockstar’s] environmental lighting is mostly dynamic and looks as good if not better than most baked lighting.”

In really, really simple terms, baked lighting is a game development technique used to save computational cost by calculating light and shadow data in advance.

The downside to this is that it’s fixed, but obviously given the ever-changing nature of GTA 6’s sandbox, it needs to have a dynamic solution.

Barclay is saying that GTA 6’s dynamic lighting matches and even surpasses those pre-determined solutions in many scenarios, making it a real accomplishment.

These comments triggered discussion from various other industry professionals, including Tim Soret from Odd Tales, the makers of The Last Night, who outlined some of his thoughts on the title:

GTA 6 sets a standard so unfathomably high I do wonder at what point it’ll ever be topped.

I suppose raising the bar like this will motivate the many other talented devs around the world, but not every studio will have access to the time and the estimated $1 billion budget that allowed Rockstar to deliver this.

Either way, it’s clear industry professionals are utterly blown away by what the studio has delivered here.

#3866. UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is more worried "about the amount of time" people will spend on GTA 6 than the game's violent content

"I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games."

Leader of the UK Conservative Party (and former Mortal Kombat player) Kemi Badenoch is more worried about the amount of time people will spend playing GTA 6 rather than the game itself.

Every new Grand Theft Auto game invites some amount of controversy over its in-game violence or depictions of sex and drugs - from San Andreas' raunchy Hot Coffee mini-game to GTA 5's graphic torture scene. Ahead of GTA 6's release this week, the Tory leader downplayed those fears.

"I would be more worried about the amount of time people were spending on a game than the game specifically. I remember in my childhood playing Mortal Kombat and Street Fighter. I didn't hit anybody after playing those games," Badenoch said in a news conference shared by Sky News (good spot, IGN).

While Badenoch's stance might be surprising for the normally right-wing UK political party, she did still worry over children who might play GTA 6 for too long. There are probably far worse ways for kids to spend their time than engaging with a long-form story like GTA 6's, though, especially in an era with endless amounts of 10-second clips to mindlessly scroll past and declining funding into youth programs.

"I haven't played Grand Theft Auto, I know people are worried about the game content. At the same time, I'd be more worried about a kid who played it all day, who was in their bedroom all day, than one who spends half an hour on it and then went out and did something else. They are two different things," Badenoch added.

GTA 6's release is imminent and is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time. One analyst even suggested GTA 6 could make over $2bn in its opening weekend - that's handily more money than Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey made during its entire run in cinemas, for context.

If you'd like to reminisce a bit before the long-awaited game finally hits, you can check out our favourite Grand Theft Auto pieces Eurogamer's published over the years.

#3865. Original GTA 6 leaker pleads guilty to hacking Rockstar Games, years after first revealing Lucia

The 21-year-old responsible for hacking Rockstar Games and leaking in-development GTA 6 footage in 2022 has pleaded guilty to a number of offenses.

The GTA 6 leaker was initially sentenced to an indefinite stay at a hospital due to his severe autism, but was more recently deemed fit for trial and moved to a regular prison earlier this January. On Monday, at the Woolwich Crown Court in South East London, he pleaded guilty to hacking Rockstar Games and a number of other companies, including Uber and EE/BT, in cyber attacks estimated to have caused £10m in damages.

At the time of his Rockstar hack - when he was between the ages of 16 and 17 - the leaker was already under police protection at a Travelodge hotel to keep him from rival hackers he had allegedly stolen Bitcoin from. Somewhat surprisingly, he then managed to hack the multi-billion dollar game maker with nothing but an Amazon Fire Stick, the hotel room's TV and a bluetooth-connected keyboard and mouse.

As the BBC reports, he also managed to break into the developer's Slack channels, before threatening to release the GTA 6 source code if Rockstar failed to contact him within the day. The leaker has yet to be sentenced.

Those 2022 leaks were quite substantial, too, revealing about an hour of unfinished gameplay and clueing the world in on Lucia's existence - the series' first female protagonist in years. Of course, those 2022 leaks shouldn't be confused with 2026's, which saw Cyberleek spill nuggets of nearly finished clips onto the internet, despite Rockstar's best efforts to keep GTA 6 a closely guarded secret.

"We recently suffered a network intrusion in which an unauthorised third-party illegally accessed and downloaded confidential information from our systems, including early development footage for the next Grand Theft Auto," Rockstar said at the time, before it had officially unveiled GTA 6. "At this time we do not anticipate any disruption to our live game services, nor any long-term effect on the development of our ongoing projects. We are extremely disappointed to have any details of our next game shared with you all in this way."

Four years later, GTA 6 is finally around the corner - you're probably already aware considering the marketing frenzy Rockstar's been drumming up.

#3864. Conan: The Black Pyramid shoves the titular barbarian into a very Hades-inspired action roguelite with the addition of a few other familiar heroes

I feel like one thing I only sort of miss from my youth, viewed through the lenses of those rose tinted goggles, is the established intellectual property game that just copies the formula of another, successful game. Obviously there are plenty of genres that are trendy to imitate, but how often do you see something that's just sort of "thing you know slapped on top of game you know?" Perhaps that's a tad mean, but I do genuinely have a fondness for such games, so I'm quite pleased by the announcement of Conan: The Black Pyramid, an action roguelite RPG that so clearly went to Supergiant Games' School of Hades you have to admire the boldness just a little bit.

Conan: The Black Pyramid puts you in the hotseat as the titular barbarian, of course, but also as other characters from the series like Solomon Kane, Dark Agnes, and apparently, more! So, immediately, a notable enough difference from Hades, and one that seems like a neat take. As one of them you then "Descend into eldritch chambers of the Black Pyramid, a mysterious and dangerous place that defies the logic of space and time. Confront the shadows of the champions themselves and piece together the dark secrets of their past."

Where it is similar to Hades lies in the fact that the titular triangle changes in form each time you go in it, and of course there are different abilities and buffs to pick up along the way to aid you in your quest. Each character has their own combination of weapons and abilities, so it does sound like you can mix it up quite nicely. There is, also, 2-player online co-op (sorry to the couch lovers, I suppose), adding to the ways it differs and making it a tad more friendly for those that have exactly one friend who also loves Conan.

Overall, seems like a fresh enough take on Hades while still trying to find some amount of its own identity. And hey, Hades is great, so I'm never upset about having a little bit more of that kind of game. No release date attached to Conan: The Black Pyramid just yet, but it is planned to arrive sometime in 2027. You can check it out on Steam here.

#3863. Random: GTA 6 Hides An Adorable Mario & Luigi Easter Egg In Its Massive World

After 13 long years, Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally out and breaking records left, right, and centre. While folks who only own a Switch or Switch 2 can't get in on the action, we can at least appreciate a good Easter Egg when we see one.

Case in point, the game contains a pretty blatant nod to Mario and Luigi if you know where to look. As highlighted by TheGamingRevolution on YouTube, heading to Lummox County in the north of Leonida and locating a ruined site in the countryside will yield a pair of hats that look remarkably similar to the attire made famous by Nintendo's brotherly mascots.

Essentially, at the top of the ruins, you'll notice a near-invisible block floating just above the main structure. Reaching the top and then jumping into the block will cause it to burst, revealing two hats: one is red with the letter 'J' adorned for Jason, and the other green with the letter 'L' for Lucia.

It's a lovely little nod to Nintendo, and one that we suspect most people will never see. It clearly showcases Rockstar Games' appreciation for Nintendo and its games, and it's a stark contrast to the sheer stupidity we've seen recently with so-called 'fans' review-bombing games over on Metacritic.

In case you missed it, GTA 6 has found itself being review-bombed by folks claiming it to be 'woke' while lamenting the lack of 60fps. Some people, however, seemingly believe that Nintendo fans are to blame for the low scores, and so have taken it upon themselves to do the same to Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2, lowering its once record-breaking user score of 9.6 down to 8.3.

@Lizuka The recent Xbox "glitch" has shown that the game isn't as CPU-intensive as initially thought. It basically unlocks the game's frame rate, but keeps the game logic to 30fps, so while an Xbox Series X could be running it at 45-50fps, everything is faster like it's sped up at ~1.5x.

The Series S using this glitch has a minor improvement, though looking upwards allows it to increase the frame rate because it's not having to render as much. So in this particular case, the GPU is the bottleneck. The game forces a 720p native render before upscaling to 1080p, and there is no dynamic resolution scaling to lessen the load. The idea was that a Witcher 3 solution could be used by shifting CPU tasks to the GPU. With seeing the CPU utilization not being as heavy as once thought, it makes it that much more valid to use this trick, especially on simulations that don't need immediately reactions.

A hypothetical Switch 2 version would not need to render at 720p. They could render as low as 540p if needed (docked), reducing GPU and RAM bandwidth utilization, and then upscale to 1080p with DLSS. Use of dedicated RT cores will help as well because they are not only more complete, but can run concurrently with rendering. Series S uses RDNA 2, which digs into the GPU shader and TMU resources, cutting into the render budget because it can't be don concurrently.

Honestly, Series S tends to get the lazy treatment from developers, but Rockstar is not one of those. If they are willing to put in the time to craft a Series S version to look as good as it does, then they should be capable of making a good Switch 2 version.

#3862. Report: Major Details Revealed About Xbox's Original Plan For Project Helix

"Xbox Helix’s original plan was far more radical than we knew"

We've been hearing about Xbox's Project Helix console for some time now, with Xbox always talking very vaguely about what we can expect from it, and perhaps that's because the vision has changed for the system over the years.

Today, the folks over at Windows Central are revealing details about the "original plan" for Xbox Project Helix, which include that it was going to be a "full gaming PC" akin to the ROG Xbox Ally with the ability to run console games on top. Steam support would have been included, as would have Windows 11 in general.

They were seemingly even going to drop the paywall for multiplayer games in the process.

"The original plan for Helix, which ran under a different codename until last summer, was for it to essentially be a full gaming PC with the capability to run all of your existing Xbox console games on top. It would be functionally similar to the Xbox Ally PC gaming handheld, with a gamepad-first Xbox-style full-screen interface, complete with the capability to exit out to the Windows desktop and install whatever you want. That, indeed, included Steam.

As part of this strategy, Xbox would have had no choice but to drop the paywall for multiplayer from Xbox Game Pass (formerly Xbox Live Gold). There's no universe where a true PC could function with a multiplayer paywall. I understand that, indeed, removing the paywall was costed into this strategy."

All of this was apparently conceived prior to the component crisis that's caused hardware prices to rise significantly in recent times, and ultimately there's a feeling that the plan might have changed somewhat as a result.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has also become the head of the brand since Helix was in the conception phase, and she may have her own ideas about dropping multiplayer paywalls and integrating Steam into the next-gen console. After all, a lot of people have wondered what Xbox stands to gain by partnering with Steam instead of focusing on the Xbox Store.

It's important to highlight here that nobody knows what the current plan is at Xbox HQ, and Windows Central theorises that "maybe Microsoft doesn't even know itself". There's every chance we still may be looking at a console that can run Steam games and not require a multiplayer paywall, but there's probably an equal chance that Xbox has gone back the drawing board and decided to reel in its scope when it comes to PC support.

Let's wait and see, eh? We know we're definitely getting the ability to play PC titles on Xbox Project Helix no matter what, but the safe bet is that it'll be via the Xbox Store - and who knows what'll happen with the multiplayer side of things.

For what it's worth, Xbox has this month committed to Helix being a console and not a PC, which seemingly goes against the original plan for a so-called "full gaming PC". In that regard, it appears that things have changed.

"We're very clear on the design goal: Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games. The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access my games. But if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customizability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it."

Fraser is the News Editor at Pure Xbox, where he spends his time reporting on the biggest stories in the world of Xbox and beyond.

I have said time and time and time again that it makes no sense whatsoever for Microsoft to release a console that is essentially a PC that provides access to the likes of Steam. None whatsoever! And of course, I have had an enormous amount of pushback from some people on these forums.

I have said time and time again that people would simply switch to buying their games on Steam because they are cheaper there. Even now, a quick look on Loaded at Steam at games that are coming out on Steam and Xbox shows:

*Stranger Than Heaven Deluxe Edition £79.99 on the Xbox Store, and £64.99 on Steam. A saving of £15. *Persona 4 Revival Premium Edition £84.99 on the Xbox Store, and £69.99 on Steam. A saving of £15. *Metro 2039 Standard Edition £59.99 on the Xbox Store, and £40.49 on Steam. A saving of 19.50. *Dragon Quest Monsters: The Withered World Digital Deluxe Edition, which is £79.99 on the Xbox Store and £61.49 on Steam. A saving of 18.50.

These are not guesses on my part. They can be looked up right now. So if you were interested in buying each of these 4 games, you would save £68.00 by doing so on Steam, which means you would have saved enough to buy a fifth game. So why would you buy these games on Xbox? And let's not forget, when Steam has a sale, they undercut the Xbox Store then too meaning you can save even more still.

Again, I have said before that if Helix offers PC game play, then they have to drop the online paywall. Even if Helix only offers access to the Microsoft Store, then they will have to drop the online paywall because that is already the case for those that currently buy games through the Microsoft Store, and it is why PC Games Pass is cheaper as it takes into account that there is no online paywall on PC.

Problem is, most of us that have Essential only do so because it is, well... essential to have if you want to play online. Get rid of the online paywall and many of us will no longer need Essential, so a whole swathe of people will suddenly abandon Game Pass. And I'd wager there are a lot of people that would leave Premium and Ultimate too. Right now some will only have those tiers because they are better than Essential, but they really only want online access. Make that free, and then the imperative of having Games Pass is gone, and if they don't feel they are getting value from the service, then they too can quit without losing access to online play.

I know a lot of people really want Helix to be a PC that offers access to Steam, but honestly, they really need to be careful about what they wish for, because as I have said many times now, Steam will be the downfall of Xbox because once people see what savings they can make on Steam Microsoft will lose billions in revenue...

One last thing, as I have said before, if Helix offers PC gaming including access to Steam, then I do not think Microsoft will be able to subsidise it at all. The reason is fairly simple; if Helix is seen as a decent entry point PC, and it is subsidised making it significantly cheaper than it would be to build a similar PC yourself, then people will buy it to use as a Steam machine. They will completely sidestep the Xbox Store. That would mean that not only would Microsoft be selling Helix at a loss, but also they would not make a penny from those that bought it. The only reason the likes of Microsoft and Sony subsidise consoles right now is because they make back the losses on the price of the console through sales on their Stores. So, if Helix is essentially a PC Microsoft will sell it either for the cost of making it, or with a slight profit.

Sony, on the other hand, can subsidise the PS6 because they will be locking their customers into buying games through the PlayStation Store.

So, if Helix were to cost £1000 to make, then the least that Microsoft would sell it for would be £1000. If the PS6 costs the same to make, then Sony could subsidise it and see it cost £900 or even £800.

Thing is, if Helix really is a PC capable device, then it is likely to cost much more than £1000 meaning the gap in between Helix and the PS6 could be far greater than £200.

So if the PS6 is sold for £800 (and I think that is what Sony will aim for), and Helix is sold for £1200 (and I think it could be more than that as PC components are not cheap) then that is a difference of £400, and that difference maybe enough to persuade a not insignificant number of people to switch from Xbox to PlayStation.

Obviously, I have no idea what Helix will be. I have no idea of how much either Helix or the PS6 will be sold at. I just know that enabling us to purchase games through and for Steam on Helix will be absolutely disastrous for Xbox, and so I really hope they have the sense to change course and no give us access to it as I want to be gaming on an Xbox for many generations yet...

#3861. Star Wars: Galactic Racer is getting much-requested split-screen multiplayer and new mode in 2027

The surprisingly awesome arcade podracing game Star Wars: Galactic Racer is getting split-screen multiplayer next year after loud fan requests, developer Fuse Games has announced.

Split-screen racing comes as part of an entirely new mode called Free Play that'll also allow players to mix and match vehicles, characters, tracks and planets in a galaxy far, far away. So, maybe don't expect to bring friends into the game's vast, pre-existing suite of modes just yet.

"We heard you," the studio wrote on social media. "Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at Fuse Games has been working hard to bring a brand new mode, Free Play, to Star Wars: Galactic Racer. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action."

We’ve heard you! Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at @Fuse_Games has been working hard to bring a brand new mode, Free Play, to STAR WARS: Galactic Racer™. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action.

Galactic Racer already has a pretty good selection of online multiplayer modes, like the 12-player speeder races and 8-player podracing tours, but there's currently no way to play with your mates in the same room.

Chris Donlan loved the thrilling racing game for mixing the best bits of Star Wars and Burnout - Fuse Games does have plenty of old Criterion DNA, mind you. "It's new games, with Roguelite choices and endless unlockables, and it's also old games, with cruel and ingenious courses where everything can be lost in an instant. It's a Galaxy Far, Far Away, and it's also Paradise City," he wrote in Eurogamer's five-star review.

With Galactic Racer and Zero Company under its belt, Lucasfilm Games said it's now "more flexible" about which developers it accepts pitches from. Hopefully, that'll lead to even more interesting games set in Star Wars' ultra flexible world.

#3860. GTA 6 Just Can't Stop Breaking Records It Seems

Sets new soundtrack streaming record on Spotify

Not content with being the biggest entertainment launch in history and the highest rated game of all time, GTA 6 has already broken another record.

The game’s official album, which features all-new tracks from the likes of Dua Lipa, set a new opening day record for a soundtrack on Spotify with a dizzying 29.85 million streams.

The compilation has 34 songs, including music from artists like Travis Scott, Morgan Wallen, and Jennie.

#3859. EA really doesn't want you to delete Madden NFL 27 to make room for GTA 6

"Don't let 210GB get between you and your league."

Assuming you didn't just buy a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S to play Grand Theft Auto 6, your console's limited storage space is likely already strained, meaning tough choices may have to be made to make room for Rockstar's chonky 212GB crime game.

In a move I don't remember seeing before, EA is asking players to spare Madden NFL 27 from the purge to free up console storage space. As spotted by Push Square, a desperate in-game message pops up when you launch the American Football game, pleading with you not to delete it.

The message highlights 17th November as the date of a Madden NFL 27 update, though its styling, wording and choice of background seem to hint at GTA 6.

"Don't delete!" it reads, as shared by Zirksee on X. "[Encrypted Signal] The target is locked. The crew is assembling for a high-stakes run. Await the signal from our insider on 11/17… do not leak this transmission."

EA's language and intention, however, are much clearer in this post on X, which specifically references GTA 6's large file size in a cheeky way, seemingly promoting the same update.

"Don't let 210GB get between you and your league," the post reads, clearly quoting GTA 6's file size.

The update in question is fairly notable, adding a Madden 97 throwback with era-appropriate players, playbooks and what looks to be 16-bit visuals. Though it's obviously not related to GTA 6 in any way, it's easy to see why EA would fear a significant drop in players once Rockstar's game arrives, something other publishers are undoubtedly worried about.

As part of a recent restructuring, EA laid off 400 employees, closed down BioWare, cancelled unannounced projects and revealed a refocusing on its core franchises and biggest monkey-makers. That includes EA Sports, of course, where a team is currently developing a game codenamed Project Gridiron, described as "a social-first open-world experience for our American Football team".

#3858. Opinion: After Finishing Ocarina Of Time, I'm Left Jonesing For A Proper Sequel

Yesterday I finished the Ocarina of Time remake. Having replayed the original over the summer with my kids, we've beansed it through this one, taking our time to enjoy the view and appreciate the myriad changes, but already knowing exactly where to go and what to do.

What is there left to say about it? It's an excellent video game, a thoroughly impressive revamp which changes enough to feel modern without trampling over the original. I have a handful of tiny issues with it (the Sheik reveal always felt a bit obvious, but here I don't see how anybody won't see it coming), but they're minuscule in the scheme of things. Childhoods haven't been ruined, and at a time when genuine warm fuzzies are in short supply, Nintendo has delivered.

Still, after catching the Loach and using the in-game menus to track down the last Skulltulas and Heart Pieces — and even dipping into Zelda Notes and OCD-ing every last rupee-filled Treasure Chest for the magic 100% rating in the app — I was left feeling a tad...deflated? That's not quite the word, but there was an emptiness.

It's a stunning game and I enjoyed every second, but as a remake it naturally lacked the same sense of wonder you get from exploring and not knowing what's around the next corner. Delight up the wazoo, but not so much in the 'surprise' department.

The natural conclusion, given the very warm reception and impressive sales, is that Nintendo will crack straight on with Majora's Mask next. And yes, absolutely; MM is my personal favourite, so of course I'll take a remake. It's the least-brainer-y no-brainer since Ocarina 3D was a hit.

However, already knowing the world and the story does take something away from the Zelda experience, and having now appreciated this remake's gorgeous art style, the presentation would provide less novelty next time, too.

"It's not as exciting when you know what's coming," said my seven-year-old last night after we rolled credits. Both kids still sat beside me for "30 hours or more" over the past three weeks, mind, so let's not blow this out of proportion. I could feel her attention wandering at times, though, even with the grandeur of the visuals and all the additions.

So, I've now got a dilemma. Do I show them the original Majora's Mask as planned, or wait for the hypothetical remake and preserve its narrative twists and turns? Would they prefer to be surprised? Despite wanting to see the Zora mask in action, they'd both rather wait. Saying they'll be old enough to control it themselves in a couple of years may have soured them on watching me play the "square-y" version now. Fingers crossed Nintendo actually makes the thing.

The parent's perspective isn't a consideration for everyone, it's just an interesting conundrum. I'm also aware that none of this is an issue for Ocarina newbies! For me personally, though, as much as I would/will devour Majora's Mask, there's another approach that could bring the best of both worlds. A link, ahem, between worlds, if you will. What about a brand new sequel to Ocarina?

Imagine a game which continues the Hero of Time's journey, with Link grown up — in his mid-20s, say — exploring a Hyrule changed by his heroics in the first game. This Link saved Hyrule and Termina, and (almost) nobody in his world knows it. That's fertile ground for a story only hinted at in Twilight Princess.

The Ocarina remake gives glimpses of a larger world beyond Hyrule's hills. How about a sequel that lets us explore those, expanding the horizons and pushing out the frontiers of this contained kingdom? A game which taps our emotional connections and nostalgia but brings something truly unknown as well.

Could that be it? Could that integration of old and new — Ocarina + BOTW — be a direction for the series as a whole? Mashing two known ideas to make something notionally fresh is fandom 101, of course. "What if Ocarina but bigger?" "What if old Link travelled back with a warning!" "What if Dark Link was a premonition and the Hero of Time has to save Hyrule from his own ego!" It's easy to pump out the 'what ifs'.

It's also easy to say, "Oh, just put old-school Ocarina-like dungeons into the open world!" It's a design headache, to be sure, but also a problem Nintendo has the know-how to tackle.

I just feel like there's more gold to mine from this world and this engine beyond a straightforward Majora's Mask remake. I'd play that and love it, the same as if they announced A Link to the Past or a reimagined version of the NES original. But I have played those games already - a vital element of the Zelda formula is missing in any remake.

Not feeling like a 'stopgap' project to train up staff while Aonuma and co. work out how the hell to follow up Tears of the Kingdom is one of this remake's most impressive qualities. We've already asked the question about whether that open-world Hyrule could withstand a third entry, and a direct sequel to TOTK seems unlikely. In some ways, remaking The Best Game of All Time was a mighty clever distraction.

However, if Nintendo doesn't have some revolutionary new take on Zelda up its sleeve just yet, I'd love to see them exploit this Hyrule and explore this Link's story some more. The last time they told a new story with a Link from long ago, we got the sublime A Link Between Worlds. Yes. Yes, please.

Let us know below how you'd feel about more adventures in strange new (and old) worlds with the Hero of Time, whether that's revisiting Termina or something else entirely.

#3857. Warhammer 40,000: Darktide's next class is the Sisters Novitiate, a group who love staking and burning people for the God-Emperor, and its out next month

Look at you, you lucky devil, you're being treated to a new Warhammer 40,000: Darktide class next month! This class is called the Sisters Novitiate, a group of wonderfully violent women with a penchant for crossbows, burning people alive and putting a stop to anyone that dares to oppose the God-Emperor. Neato!

According to a blog post accompanying the reveal of the class, the Sisters Novitiate work a tad differently compared to other classes available in the game. "Unlike other classes, the Sisters Novitiate are able to choose from six divine and devastating Acts of Faith, as opposed to blitz and combat abilities," the post explains. "Their abilities draw upon reserves of Faith, allowing them to unleash brutal Neural Whip attacks to the inspiring Icon of Purity and protective prayers. Faith can take many forms for the Sisters Novitiate, each channeling the Emperor's divine will and bringing his wrath upon his enemies."

You build up their Faith while fighting, in turn choosing from a selection of doctrines and pledges in their talent tree, "each shaping how Faith is both accumulated and put to use. Any two Acts of Faith can be equipped at a time, allowing players to choose how their Novitiate will unleash righteous fury on the battlefield." I mentioned crossbows, right? Well, I stand lore corrected, as what they technically have is the Condemnor Stakethrower, which "pins what remains of their enemies to the walls." They do also have access to a flamethrower, a big ole mace, your classic sword and shield, and whatever the hell a "Penitent Eviscerator."
